articles.title: 8 Ways Doing a Genealogy DNA Test Can Come Back to Bite You—And Even Cause Legal Problems
articles.content:
We’ve all heard the feel-good stories about DNA testing exonerating the wrongly accused, catching a killer or reuniting long-lost relatives. These situations are often framed by local news anchors and law enforcement as triumphs of technology, and sometimes they are. But voluntarily submitting your DNA to a genealogy testing company—as 21% of Americans have, according to a 2025 YouGov poll—can have unintended consequences.
I can hear you thinking: What could be the harm? I’m not a criminal! And I would love to meet my fourth cousin twice removed! Of course, a family reunion sounds fun (and hopefully you’re not on the FBI’s Most Wanted list), but once you give that spit or swab sample over to one of those companies, the “good” and “bad” tentacles of DNA testing can be impossible to untangle.
“Nobody is against catching serial killers,” says Natalie Ram, a professor of law at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law whose research focuses on genetic privacy and how it intersects with the criminal legal system. “But privacy is also a really important human value—and an American legal value, in particular.”
I spoke with Ram and Fadi Matthew Kazandji, a criminal defense lawyer and founder and managing partner at Kazandji Law in Canada, to understand the risks of genealogical testing. What could go wrong when you submit your sample to one of these companies? Quite a bit, actually, so read on.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more genealogy, news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Whether you spit in a cup or swab your cheek, once you send off your sample to a genealogical testing company, “they typically hold onto that biospecimen unless or until you request that they destroy it,” Ram says. And that’s two valuable things the company now has control over: your genetic data and the raw sample, which could be used for further sequencing at a later time.
What kind of further testing are we talking about? One likely candidate is whole-genome sequencing, which gives a much more extensive profile than the typical “genotyping” done by these companies. “The specific details of a specific platform are likely buried in the terms of service and privacy policy, so you should consult that before you use one of their kits,” Ram says.
But, as you’ll see coming up, reading the terms isn’t a fail-safe.
“You should also know that it is extremely common, across the internet, including on these consumer genetics platforms, for a vendor to reserve the right to change the terms of service and privacy policy at any time,” Ram says. “Your continued use of the service, which means your non-deletion of your account, is considered consent to the updated terms.”
And sometimes the companies themselves don’t necessarily think the terms through. She points to the 23andMe bankruptcy from 2025: The company had recently updated their terms to allow the sale of consumer data, but didn’t address the actual physical specimens. That left a kind of “gray zone” about what might happen to them.
“One thing that is quite common in the consumer genetic space is that companies, in their terms of service and privacy policies, often take great pains to say your genetic data is yours,” Ram says. “Which, on the one hand, sounds great. On the other hand, [it] doesn’t actually provide a lot of robust protection.”
She cautions people “not to be wooed” by the language of ownership. Your data and sample may be your “property,” but property rights are not absolute. They’re affected by what you’ve consented to allow others to do with it, which again, is buried in the fine print. “The terms of service will say ‘this is your data,’ but you also grant us all of the rights to do thus and such with it,” Ram says.
This is the one most people are worried about, Ram says, and there have been multiple instances of hacking and other breaches at these companies. A particularly worrisome one affected 23andMe customers of Asian and Ashkenazi Jewish heritage, whose data was sold on the dark web.
The state of California sued 23andMe over this exposure in May 2026. “The sale of this data on the dark web took place amidst a period of mounting anti–Asian American and Pacific Islander and anti-Semitic hate and violence—and explicitly called attention to the deeply personal and identifying nature of that information,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said when announcing the suit.
Remember that unlike a credit card number, you can’t get new DNA. “So once it’s fallen into dark-web hands, it’s there forever and you can’t change it, no matter what,” Ram says.
You’ve probably heard of the Golden State Killer, who eluded capture for decades until 2018, when investigators uploaded a DNA sample to something called GEDmatch. That’s a free database that allows users to upload their genetic data so it can be accessed and searched by others to look for matches.
“Since then, over 1000 cases have been investigated using what is now called forensic investigative genetic genealogy, or FIGG,” Ram says. You might think this is good news (killers off the streets!), but she warns that law enforcement doesn’t always play by the rules and is “largely unburdened by law” in this space.
Let’s say the police are looking for a suspect and they have a DNA sample from a crime scene. “Rather than saying, ‘Hi, I’m law enforcement, and I’d like to search for suspects in your database,’ they will instead pretend to be an ordinary user and say, ‘This is my data,'” Ram says.
After a series of scandals, Ram says GEDmatch created a portal for law enforcement and gave users the option to opt out of allowing investigators to comb through their genetic info. But both law enforcement and genetic genealogists have been caught using loopholes to get around these privacy restrictions.
When 23andMe filed for bankruptcy protection in 2025, the company sold the genetic data of its 15 million–plus users to a new nonprofit created by 23andMe’s co-founder. But the first bidder was a pharmaceutical company called Regeneron, prompting worries from consumers about what they would do with the data and samples.
“It’s unclear whether they were most interested in the user data or the biospecimens, [which] would include not only the information that has already been developed but also all the other information that 23andMe, or whatever platform you’re using, didn’t even sequence yet,” Ram says.
“I am less concerned with insurers trying to get access to these platforms,” Ram says. “I am more concerned about insurers conditioning your ability to get important forms of insurance, like life, long-term-care and disability insurance, based on genetic risks that you knew about because you used one of these services.”
Congress did enact the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA), which protects against discrimination in employment and health insurance under many circumstances. The Affordable Care Act has similar protections. But neither law applies to life, long-term-care and disability insurance, leaving states to create a patchwork of protections.
Kazandji says Canada’s laws are more robust. “It’s a crime here to make someone take a genetic test, or hand over results from one they already took, as a condition of selling them something or signing a contract with them,” he says. “That includes insurance and jobs. The maximum is five years in jail and a $1 million fine, and the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the law in 2020.”
Maybe it sounds exciting to trace your family history, or smart to research potential medical issues in your family tree. But there can be downsides, not the least of which is learning something you wish you hadn’t. “Misattributed paternity is surprisingly common—much more common that people realize,” Ram says. You could learn you have half-siblings, or adoptions that were never disclosed to the family.
Before you use these services, Ram says it’s also important to grapple with the fact that the data you’re sharing is not just your data. “It’s the data of dozens, hundreds or even thousands of other individuals” to whom you’re genetically related. On the other side of the issue, that means even if you haven’t taken one of these tests, your data may still be out there regardless.
It’s easy to say “just don’t take the test,” and that’s one thing to consider. But if you do decide the benefits outweigh the risks, Ram and Kazandji have some advice.
Yes, but slowly, and not always in the direction of stronger privacy.
Ram is very proud of the work she’s done in her state to get protections on the books: “The Maryland law says when law enforcement approaches a person they know to be an innocent third party, to ask them to cooperate in an investigation, they are not allowed to lie.”
Utah is another state that has enacted a “relatively comprehensive regulatory scheme,” Ram says, though it’s less robust than Maryland’s. And Montana has a short statute that requires law enforcement to get a warrant before gaining access to DNA databases.
As for the overall trend with these laws? “I do not have high hopes that they will provide genuine data protection vis-à-vis the government,” Ram says.

articles.title: TSA Experts Answer: Can You Wear Your Halloween Costume on a Plane?
articles.content:
Debate time: Would you wear a Halloween costume on a flight? Would you look askance at someone who did? What if they sat right next to you or draped their Morticia Addams wig all over your tray table from the next row up? I have not had the pleasure of sitting next to a costumed Halloween reveler, and due to my rather reserved personality, I can’t imagine wearing one myself, but hey—you be you!
‘Tis the season for fall travel, and during this last stretch of October, there are bound to be people all over this country wondering if the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) will even let them dress up for Halloween on their flights. So, to help all you outgoing types plan around the spooky season, I checked in with someone who knows what he’s talking about: a former TSA official.
“I can tell you that TSA officers have seen just about everything come through a security checkpoint,” says Keith Jeffries, a 20-year veteran of the TSA who is now a vice president at K2 security consultants. “Halloween just makes things a little more interesting.” Ahead, Jeffries and Daniel D. Velez, a current spokesman for the TSA, explain what is and definitely isn’t allowed on planes this Halloween.
Read on to learn what you can wear, what you should pack and what you should leave at home.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
“Absolutely—you can wear a Halloween costume on a flight!” Jeffries says. “TSA doesn’t want to take the fun out of Halloween. The key is making sure your costume doesn’t create a security concern or slow down the screening process.”
As Jeffries mentioned, security is where you’re likely to run into trouble if you show up looking like Vecna from Stranger Things. And being pulled aside for extra screening because you aren’t recognizable as a human being or you’re channeling The Texas Chainsaw Massacre isn’t going to be a good time for anyone (especially the people behind you).
“Halloween is supposed to be scary, but getting through airport security shouldn’t be,” Jeffries says. “My advice is simple: Dress up if you are into the Halloween spirit, but dress to get through security.” Make sure your costume complies with TSA rules (more on that coming up), and be ready to follow any instructions from TSA officers. If you have to take something off, make sure you have room in your bag or time to check it. The last thing you want to do is miss your flight.
“Remember, TSA officers are focused on keeping everyone safe, regardless of whether you’re dressed as a business traveler or Batman,” Jeffries says. “Even superheroes must follow TSA screening procedures. Batman doesn’t get to skip security.”
The main ones are weapons. “Leave the swords, knives, toy guns and realistic-looking weapons and explosive devices at home, or pack permitted costume props in your checked baggage,” Jeffries says. “Even if it’s part of a Halloween costume, anything that looks like a weapon can create a security concern.”
Other items may not be prohibited, but they still have to comply with TSA rules. Here’s what could get you flagged by airport security:
An important reminder: “TSA officers are required to treat potential threats seriously, even on Halloween,” Jeffries says. “If your costume jingles, rattles or lights up like a Christmas tree, don’t be surprised if it gets some extra attention at security.”
It could definitely slow you down. “It’s perfectly fine to dress like a vampire, zombie or your favorite superhero, but TSA still needs to verify your identity,” Jeffries says. “If your costume includes a full-face mask or heavy makeup that makes you difficult to recognize, be prepared to remove the mask or make adjustments so TSA officers can confirm who you are—which can slow down the security process.”
Velez takes it a little further. “Passengers should avoid wearing masks and not have painted faces when going through security screening,” he says. “Officers still need to match travelers to their ID pictures.”
You’d hate to have to take off your Bride of Frankenstein fright wig or wipe off your carefully applied Joker face right when you get to the head of that massive security line. TSA allows colored contacts, but there’s not a lot of guidance on extreme eye-color deviations. So do yourself a favor and wait till you get to your destination to go all-in. And if you’re wearing a mask, stash it in your carry-on or pack it in your luggage.
“TSA needs to know who’s behind the mask,” Jeffries says. (Or the makeup, for that matter.) “Save the big reveal for the Halloween party, not the security checkpoint.”
“The best thing passengers can do is be prepared,” Jeffries says. “Remove bulky costume accessories before screening, keep prohibited items out of carry-on bags and follow the TSA officer’s instructions.” Check the TSA website for the full list of items allowed in carry-on and checked baggage, and build in enough time to deal with any unexpected snags. If there’s any doubt, just leave the questionable item at home.
Velez advises avoiding bulky costumes altogether to get through the Advanced Imaging Technology scanners. Jeffries adds: “My recommendation is to keep your costume simple while going through security and put on the finishing touches after you’ve cleared the checkpoint.”
If you think sharing an armrest is bad, try sharing a row with a guy dressed as Edward Scissorhands. “Think about your entire travel experience, not just getting through TSA,” Jeffries says. “Large costumes, elaborate headpieces and bulky accessories can be uncomfortable on an aircraft and may interfere with other passengers.” (The last thing you want to do is scare a child on a five-hour flight—what if he starts crying?)
“Also, remember that your airline has its own rules regarding attire and what can be brought on board,” Jeffries says. Before you get all decked out, take a peek at your carrier’s website to see if they have specific rules on attire. For example, American Airlines says travelers must “dress appropriately” and not show up in bare feet (sorry, Fred Flintstone). Even if there’s not a specific rule about costumes, remember that airlines have wide latitude to keep disruptions down.
“A little preparation can keep your travel experience from becoming a horror story,” Jeffries says. “Have fun with your costume, use common sense and remember that security is serious business—even when you’re dressed as a clown.”

What else should you keep in mind about wearing a costume on a plane?

If you think sharing an armrest is bad, try sharing a row with a guy dressed as Edward Scissorhands. “Think about your entire travel experience, not just getting through TSA,” Jeffries says. “Large costumes, elaborate headpieces and bulky accessories can be uncomfortable on an aircraft and may interfere with other passengers.” (The last thing you want to do is scare a child on a five-hour flight—what if he starts crying?)

articles.content:

We also know that once you get hooked on something, you can’t stop, so you’ll be binge-watching all seven movies in a single weekend. (Don’t even try to deny it.)
Finally, Aries is ruled by Mars, the planet of war, sex and vengeance, and the movies are all about personal vendettas, painful memories, and plans to frame innocent bystanders. You can’t cheat Mother Nature by speeding up the time it takes plants to grow or, let’s say, defy death by creating a monster. Obviously, Victor Frankenstein didn’t get the memo, and you’ll gleefully watch as he’s taken down.
Beyond that, you’ll love the whole vibe of Frankenstein, no matter which version you choose. The 1931 original exudes an old-school feel with its gorgeous black-and-white cinematography, while 2025’s adaptation features moody tones and a more traditional take on Mary Shelley’s story. Both are wins in your book. And, as a master of patience, you’ll marvel at the intensive 10-hour process it took to turn Jacob Elordi into the Creature … and also won’t mind the fact that the movie is two-and-a-half hours long!
There’s one major theme in Hocus Pocus that is decidedly “Gemini,” and that’s strong bonds with your besties. Ruled by the Twins, Gemini is one of the most social signs of the zodiac, and you feel confident and powerful when you’re with your crew. That’s why you’ll be completely delighted to see the Sanderson sisters needle and joke around with one another, as well as watch Max and Dani’s sweet connection bloom.
All seriousness aside, there’s actually next to no seriousness in this movie, just the way Gemini likes it. You do, however, love some good satire, and the quote that comes to mind is Winifred’s: “Oh, look! Another glorious morning. This one will magically hit the sweet spot.

Not only are the costumes and make up expertly extravagant, but it’s also an avant-garde, gender-bending musical. Your sign rules entertainment (and live theater), which means you’ll have a blast singing along and dancing with the characters.
And why stop there? You’ll take any excuse to throw a good party, and this definitely qualifies, especially with Tim Curry’s recent passing. So grab your full makeup kit, your fishnet stockings and a string of pearls, and make this viewing party happen! (Let’s not even pretend you won’t dress up as Dr. Frank-N-Furter, who is basically your Halloween spirit animal.)
We couldn’t make a Halloween-movie list without adding this classic! And when it comes to serial-killer movies, Halloween is perfectly Virgo. Because unlike other slasher films (looking at you, Scream), Halloween pairs horror with precision. It takes fear to a cold, emotionless and calculated place—kind of like what happens when you deep-clean your house or create an itinerary for an international vacation. Think about it: Michael Myers doesn’t kill in a hot rage. (If he did, he’d be more of Mars-ruled sign like Aries.) No, Michael’s method is far more fixated and controlled.
Even the way he;s framed as the killer—a dark shape among the trees—rewards only those detail-oriented viewers who are paying close attention. The connection becomes even stronger with the haunting music in the background: slow and methodical, just like you.

articles.title: Here’s What Really Happens to Your Clothes at the Dry Cleaner
articles.content:
You bring that stained silk blouse or rumpled blazer into the dry cleaner, drop it off with the attendant at the front desk, then come back a few days later (or more if, like me, you forget) to pick up your cleaned, pressed items, hanging neatly on a hanger and wrapped in plastic. It’s a ritual that has been going on for decades, but what happens once your clothing or linens leave your hands? Do they go on a whimsical ride through dry-cleaning land, where industrious elves work their magic? Sort of! Just replace elves with launderers and finishers, and you’re close.
To get the full picture, we spoke with Mike Astorino, who has more than 34 years of experience in the business and is the owner of Fabricare, a luxury dry cleaner in Fairfield County, Connecticut. Read on to find out exactly what happens to your clothes at the dry cleaner.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
It’s all about keeping certain delicate items in tip-top shape—and cleaning them without accidentally ruining them. For those items that need this VIP treatment, the pros use solvents in place of water and traditional laundry detergent to remove stains, sweat and grime from clothing.
That said, even when a care tag says something is “dry clean only,” that doesn’t necessarily mean it is. “In general, manufacturers are careless with their labels,” Astorino says. “Big, luxury brands will put very specific care instructions onto the garment and even test fabrics before going to market. However, for the thousands of other brands out there, ‘dry clean only’ is a way for them to deny responsibility if you wash an item and it shrinks or deteriorates.” (To wit, the $12 pair of purple track pants I recently bought that are labeled “dry clean only.” I could buy a new pair for the same cost as bringing them to the cleaner’s!) In some cases, you can even wash silk and wool—if you know what you’re doing.
But certain items are essential to dry-clean, such as anything with leather trim, a loose weave that runs the risk of snagging anywhere along the process, or an item with ornamentation like crystal buttons, Astorino says.
More than you probably think! Let’s take a little trip through a dry cleaner’s shop below.
“The cleaner looks for defects, such as loose buttons, torn hems and stains, and reports them to the customer,” says Astorino. “This protects us from things we didn’t do and allows us to repair the item to return it to the customer in a wearable condition.” Then each piece gets a unique tag, which is used to track it throughout the process to ensure it doesn’t get lost.”
At Fabricare, the tag is a small sticker with a bar code that attaches to the care tag, and customers don’t typically remove it. This gives the cleaners insight into some of the garment’s history, including how often it has been dry-cleaned, as well as the date of its last cleaning.
“To simplify removal, we classify stains into two categories: plant-based, like coffee, wine or tomato sauce, and animal-based, like sweat or blood,” Astorino says. To determine which is which, common sense comes into play. “Stains in the front of the garment are usually some type of food, whereas you’re more likely to find makeup around the neck, and mud or dirt on the bottom of dresses or pants,” he explains.
Then there are invisible stains, such as perspiration, perfume or light drinks like white wine. You might not notice them, but if they’re not treated promptly, they can ruin a garment. (These are typically removed through the regular dry-cleaning process.)
Beyond the stain, the cleaner needs to consider the fabric, the dye and the condition of the item before beginning to clean.
The machine dry cleaners use is similar to the one you use at home, save for a few key differences. It doesn’t use water, and it has far more settings for temperature and speed than your home washer. “The machines are computerized for different types of loads,” Astorino says. “Delicate silks will have a gentle cycle, while heavy coats and sweaters can handle more aggressive types of cleaning.” Solvent is added directly to the machine through a hose, the same way water is introduced into your machine at home.
The other big difference? Clothes are cleaned and dried in the same machine, he explains. Just like with dry-cleaner wash cycles, there are a number of different temperature and speed options for drying.
Oh, and a single machine costs around $60,000!
If a stain didn’t come out during the first cleaning, cleaners will try a different type of solvent. At Fabricare, this happens about 30% to 40% of the time, Astorino says. As a last resort, the cleaner may need to use water, which is an aggressive cleaner. “Cleaners are trained to start with the safest stain-removal technique and gradually get more aggressive,” he says.
There comes a point when continuing to clean a garment will actually damage it, and “that’s the first thing we train cleaners [to recognize],” Astorino says. “I learned from a high-end dry cleaner in New York when I first got in the business that ‘people come to us because we know what not to clean.’ Or put another way, we know when to stop.”
If a stain won’t budge in the traditional process, Astorino’s team communicates with the customer to let them know they can’t get their garment fully clean and potentially get approval to take more aggressive steps, as detailed above.
Once an item passes the cleaning department, it goes to finishing, which means “making the garment look like it did when you bought it,” Astorino says. “This is no easy task, especially with women’s garments. It requires knowing when to steam an item versus press it, or how to block a knit back to its original look. It’s really a craft.”
This is also the step when the item gets put on a hanger.
Here’s where automation generally comes into play. At Fabricare, the unique bar code is scanned, and the item is put on a conveyor belt, aka the device that looks like a sky liner for your clothes. The system knows it has, for example, one out of three of a customer’s items. So it spits out the item, bags it and waits to pair it with the other two items to group it and return it to the customer. Chances are, your local dry cleaner has a similar conveyor belt to bring items from the cleaning and finishing area to the front, even if the process isn’t fully automated.
At home, you use laundry detergent, which emulsifies stains so they can be rinsed away by water. In dry cleaning, fabric is cleaned with a solvent. The solvent works without water, to dissolve stains chemically. “Like water, the solvent helps lift soil from the fabric, which then gets flushed out through a rinse cycle,” Astorino says.
They’re safer now than they used to be. Decades ago, dry-cleaning solvents were perchloroethylene-based (a chlorine derivative), also called PERC. The system was different too—there were separate washers and dryers, so the solvent would drip from clothing onto the floor as the item was moved to the dryer, and that floor waste was considered toxic, Astorino says. While you may have read that PERC is harmful, and is a carcinogen, the chance of freshly dry-cleaned clothing negatively impacting your health is negligible. There is some evidence, however, that PERC was harmful to workers who came into direct contact with the chemical more regularly. Still, it’s always a good idea to remove the plastic from your clothes so they can air out.
Today’s dry cleaning is more environmentally friendly as a whole, in part because the EPA passed a ruling to phase out PERC-based cleaners fully by 2034. Today’s solvents are silicone- and hydrocarbon-based, neither of which is classified as a carcinogen, and silicone solvent is the same ingredient used in many everyday skin-care products. (Fabricare has been using these types of solvents since 2009).
Plus, more and more dry cleaners are moving toward a closed-loop system, which keeps the solvent inside the machine and reuses it, to cut down on chemical emissions and waste. This means “a very high amount of solvent is reclaimed and the rest is filtered out,” Astorino says.
Just like you wouldn’t wash your jeans after every wear, you don’t need to dry clean your sweater, blouse or suit jacket every single time. And thank goodness, because dry cleaning can be pricey! That said, you do need to clean clothing before putting it away for seasonal storage—remember, most stains are invisible and will set if you leave them. (Picture yellow armpit stains on a white blouse.)
The dry-cleaning process today is actually a pretty environmentally friendly way to get your clothes clean. It uses little to no water, and the newer solvents are gentler on you and the planet.
“Almost every type of wool or silk garment can be cleaned at home,” Astorino says. Options include wet washing (handwashing items in the sink or on your machine’s gentle cycle and drying flat) or investing in a DIY dry-cleaning kit. The latter typically includes a solvent you spray on your clothes prior to steaming them in your dryer.
In terms of what to try this with, use your common sense. You’ll want to be more careful with more delicate or meaningful items, like a “lucky” sweater or anything with leather trim or sequins. As for my bargain track pants? I’ve washed and dried them several times now, and they are just fine. (Phew!)
